questions.stem: A report infers sabotage from a test failure. What is wrong?

options.text: It assumes all failures are deliberate

options.misconception: raises an alternative not the flaw

options.text: Failure alone does not establish intent

questions.explanation: Intent requires evidence of motive or action, not just a bad outcome. The tempting idea that failure implies sabotage skips alternatives like error or chance.
questions.hint: Look for direct evidence of intent.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Discrediting a claim by who produced it
questions.learningObjective: Judge evidence by content not source status
questions.stem: A reviewer dismisses data from a junior engineer. What is the flaw?

options.text: It assumes juniors are always wrong
The author's rank does not test the data

questions.explanation: Data stand or fall on their content, not on who produced them. The tempting idea that rank determines correctness confuses authority with evidence.
questions.hint: Examine the data itself.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Discrediting an argument before it is made
questions.learningObjective: Detect poisoning the well in a meeting
questions.stem: A manager calls an engineer unreliable before their proposal. What flaw?

options.text: It prejudges the proposal by attacking the presenter

questions.explanation: Discrediting a speaker in advance biases the audience against any argument they make. The proposal must be judged on content. The tempting idea that reputation predicts argument quality is bias.
questions.hint: Judge the proposal, not the person.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A possibility treated as a probability
questions.learningObjective: Avoid converting possibility into likelihood
questions.stem: A brief says a defect could occur, so it likely will. What error?

options.misconception: omits a response not the flaw

options.text: It turns possibility into likelihood without frequency data

questions.explanation: Possible and probable require different support. Without frequency data, the leap is unsupported. The tempting idea that any risk is a likely risk inflates concern.
questions.hint: Ask how often this happens.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A term doing different work in each premise
questions.learningObjective: Detect equivocation in a safety claim
questions.stem: An argument uses 'safe' for both 'meets code' and 'risk-free' in different premises. What flaw?

options.text: It assumes code is always sufficient
It proves the design exceeds code
The conclusion follows only if the senses are identical

questions.explanation: When a word shifts meaning mid-argument, the conclusion may not follow. The tempting idea that meeting code equals zero risk equivocates on 'safe'.
questions.hint: Pin down the meaning in each premise.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Judging a procedure by an outcome it produced
questions.learningObjective: Avoid outcome bias in process review
questions.stem: A procedure is praised because it produced a good build despite sloppy steps. What bias?

options.text: It judges the process by its result rather than quality

questions.explanation: A good outcome can hide a bad process. Judging procedure by result risks repeating dangerous shortcuts. The tempting idea that success excuses sloppiness is outcome bias.
questions.hint: Ask whether the steps would usually succeed.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Past expenditure offered as a reason to continue
questions.learningObjective: Reject sunk-cost reasoning in continuation decisions
questions.stem: A team continues a failing prototype because of money already spent. What flaw?

options.text: Past spending cannot recover future losses

questions.explanation: Spent funds are gone regardless. Decisions should use future costs and benefits. The tempting idea that investment obligates continuation is the sunk-cost fallacy.
questions.hint: Decide from future costs only.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: An act excused by the same act done to the group
questions.learningObjective: Detect tu quoque in an ethics note
questions.stem: A contractor excuses overbilling by saying clients overbill too. What flaw?

options.text: It excuses wrongdoing by citing others' wrongdoing

questions.explanation: Others' misconduct does not justify one's own. The reply must address the billing itself. The tempting idea that reciprocity excuses harm is tu quoque.
questions.hint: Judge the act, not the comparison.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A compromise offered as though it were balanced
questions.learningObjective: Spot false balance in a trade-off
questions.stem: A brief presents two options as equally valid though one fails all requirements. What flaw?

options.text: It gives equal weight to options with unequal support
It assumes balance is always fair

questions.explanation: Balance implies comparable support. When one option fails requirements, presenting them as peers misleads. The tempting idea that two sides always deserve equal weight is false balance.
questions.hint: Compare support, not just count sides.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What makes one account of a pattern preferable to another
questions.learningObjective: Prefer the account with greater explanatory power
questions.stem: Two engineers offer different accounts of a recurring vibration. How should the team choose?

options.text: Prefer the simpler account regardless of fit
Prefer the account from the senior engineer
Prefer the account that predicts new observations and explains more
Prefer the account that matches prior belief

questions.explanation: A better account explains more of the evidence and predicts new cases. Authority, simplicity, or prior belief alone do not suffice. The tempting idea that any one criterion decides is incomplete.
questions.hint: Test which account predicts the next case.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: The account that covers more of the period at issue
questions.learningObjective: Prefer the explanation spanning the full range
questions.stem: One account explains a failure only at peak load; another covers all load levels. Which is better?

options.text: The narrower account, because it is more precise
The broader account, because it explains more of the observed range

questions.explanation: An account that covers only part of the observed range leaves cases unexplained. The broader account is preferable unless contradicted. The tempting idea that precision beats coverage is mistaken.
questions.hint: Count the cases each account explains.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A factor named only after the result was known
questions.learningObjective: Detect post-hoc reasoning in root-cause analysis
questions.stem: After a failure, a team blames a factor they never monitored before. What flaw?

options.text: It selects a cause after seeing the result
It assumes the factor is controllable

questions.explanation: A cause proposed only after the outcome is known risks fitting the story to the result. It needs independent support. The tempting idea that hindsight identifies cause is post-hoc reasoning.
questions.hint: Ask whether the factor was predicted beforehand.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Making two accounts of one event comparable
questions.learningObjective: Align units and scope before comparing
questions.stem: Two reports describe the same outage in different units and time windows. What must be done first?

options.text: Convert to common units and matching windows before comparing

questions.explanation: Comparison requires commensurable measures. Without alignment, differences may be artifacts of measurement. The tempting idea that reports can be compared directly ignores unit and scope mismatches.
questions.hint: Make the measures comparable first.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: An elimination resting on how the data were gathered
questions.learningObjective: Question data-gathering basis of an elimination
questions.stem: A candidate cause is ruled out because sensors missed it. What weakness?

options.text: It assumes sensors are always accurate
It proves the cause is impossible
The elimination depends on sensor coverage, which may be incomplete

questions.explanation: An elimination is only as strong as the data behind it. If sensors did not cover the relevant conditions, the cause is not truly excluded. The tempting idea that absence in data equals absence in reality is weak.
questions.hint: Check what the sensors actually covered.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A pattern the analyst was already looking for
questions.learningObjective: Detect confirmation bias in an inspection report
questions.stem: An inspector finds defects matching a suspected cause and stops searching. What bias?

options.text: It stops at confirming evidence and ignores disconfirming cases

questions.explanation: A search that stops at confirming cases risks missing evidence against the hypothesis. Full evaluation requires disconfirming cases too. The tempting idea that finding expected defects proves the cause is confirmation bias.
questions.hint: Ask what would disprove the suspected cause.
